review_text_raw:
Probably the best spiritual successor to Uplink: Hacker Elite I've ever seen. As a hacking simulator it is fairly straight forward. You always know what to do and the challange lies in searching through logs and mails and "snoop around". Where Uplink had the greatest challange in hacking and cracking Hacknets hacking is pretty straight forward "activate the right program in the right order and wait".

But still - the feel and look of the game was pleasing and I had fun playing it. Took me about 8 hours in a slow pace with a cuppa and my back relaxed.

It's hard NOT to compare Hacknet with Uplink though, and if you played Uplink you might feel "locked in" in Hacknet since it's much more streamlined and linear. You can't upgrade your rig, memory, CPU or anything but the hacking is quicker and allows for more typing with autocompletion where Uplink had you clicking and an unhealthy amount of drag-and-drop.

Still, would have been nice if Hacknet had drag-and-drop in the file system. And the ability to make folders.

PROS:
Quick
Good looking
Fun
Easy to play but challenging to progress
Rewarding

CONS:
Narrow and linear gameplay
Not that much to explore
You can't upgrade your rig so you quickly run out of memory/stuff you can do at the same time
The procedurally generated missions/contracts you can accept quickly runs out and there is "only" the main story left.

Summary: Awesome game. Hoping for a sequal in the spirit of Uplink though. Hacklink, perhaps? Please?

review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] I played this offline, but i think it took somewhere around 12-24h to finish the game.
[b]Grindy Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement:[/b] Yes (8 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Developer Response:[/b] No (last response is in 26 Feb, 2019).

[h1]Intro[/h1]
Hacknet is a hacking simulator game where you have to hack some ip address with the tools you had. Most of the hacking will be done through terminal although the game has some GUI that you can interact with.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Even though i said that you'll type your commands through terminal, it doesn't mean that you'll only have to look at it. There are some UI in the game that you can see, such as when you launch your tools or check the compromised system. I even think that the UI helped very well because i'm sure i don't want to browse all of the system directory from the command line; it took too much effort to type and check them all. You can also see the server location and connect to them without typing at all in case you forgot the ip or just too lazy to type the whole thing.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The game's story is mostly told through an exchange of emails and reading files in a server. You'll investigate someone who has been lost for a long time, Bit, while uncovering a hidden secret that causes his disappearance. The story might look decent, but i'm quite impressed with the visuals at the end of the story.

The game also has additional files in the servers that you hacked in. I like to read some of them (especially the short ones) since they are pretty funny.

[h1]The game[/h1]
As a hacking simulator game, the game simulates the terminal very well. The basic is pretty much the same (ls, cd, cat, etc) while there are some custom commands mixed in. The game also has an auto complete feature although it's quite limited; you can't do auto complete for stuffs in other directory. Well, sometimes it works, but sometimes it don't. The game also doesn't support complicated command with arguments like rm -rf (remove everything in a directory) even though the game has missions like this. The limitations are pretty acceptable to me though.

Anyway, if you have no idea with anything that i said above, the game will help you to learn some terminal commands. If you're in windows, it's the thing that popped up when you press windows+r and then type cmd, except that the commands are for Linux OS and the like. Like how most terminals are, there is a help command that you can use to recognize all of the available commands and if you didn't notice it like i did, the help command actually has paging in it; you can type help 1, help 2, and help 3 to check most of the commands in the game. Most, because the help command won't tell you anything about what does your .exe file do.

Beside the basic commands, you'll also have .exe files. These files are usually what is installed in your computer and can be basically anything, from a browser to your game. However, most .exe files in this game is actually a tool that is used for hacking. You'll know how the things work if you read the instructions, which is obviously stored somewhere else. You'll usually get these .exe files by going through some servers and copying the files to your machine.

In this game, you'll need to read a lot. By a lot, i mean a lot. Really. You might need to understand some complicated stuffs or just know the general knowledge and the game will punish you severely if you don't know what are you doing. I mistook proxy servers and port for a while and i thought that i need 4 proxy servers to hack in a server although it actually asked me to open 4 ports. I got confused for a while before i noticed my mistake.

Sometimes, the game won't tell you what to do and you had to understand everything by yourself. One example is when a hacker suddenly attacked me. I didn't know what to do at that point because the tutorial (yes, there is a tutorial) only tells me how to hack.

As i said before, you'll usually hack a server. You'll have a lead in a form of ip address that you need to hack in and you'll check what you need to do to hack it. The game will usually tell you whether you have to connect to a proxy, guess a firewall, run one of your hacking tools to open a number of port required to get in, or all of them. Sometimes, the server owner will notice your break in and a timer will show up. You must finish your hacking, remove your traces, and logout before it reaches zero or you'll get a blue screen. The strange thing is, the game is a bit "buggy" on this. If you leave the server while running your hacking tools, the hacking will still be ongoing and you can do your second attempt with a head start. The stranger thing is, if the timer reach zero by the time you finish the hacking (and you haven't logged out yet), the hacking will also be finished after you deal with the blue screen and return to the server. Well, there are actually some more, but these two are the only thing that i had in my mind for now.

Since you'll use a lot of hacking tools, you might run out of memories. Some hacking tools take more memories than the others so you can't use them all at the same time. This helps to make the game more difficult although there is one place where you have to "cheat" your way through because you will never have the time to get in in the first place [spoiler](the CCC Hacksquad Filedump)[/spoiler].

The game's story has a two branching paths that will converge in the end. The other path requires you to really know what you're doing though; i won't be able to make it in if i didn't read a guide beforehand. The game also has some commands that are not available in help commands that might be useful in these cases. These additional commands are told after you beat the game and is supposed to be an additional command in case there is a new update in.

You'll mostly play the game by accepting quests and finishing them. There is also a few points in the game where you can choose the missions that you want to do. Sadly, there is a place where you can't choose them all and it kinda saddens me since it left the place with unfinished tasks.

Since you'll be hacking a lot of servers, there are some optional places that you can go to and some places might have some secrets in it. I had fun locating a lot of new servers that are not introduced in the main story although i'm not sure if i got all of them; sometimes, the secret is so well hidden that you have to read really carefully.

Pros:
- Uses mostly real terminal commands
- 2 branching paths
- Lots of secrets to explore

Cons:
- Leaving the server during a trace is kinda buggy
- You need to read a lot

[h1]Conclusions[/h1]
This is a nice hacking simulation game to spend your time with.

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to play hacking simulation game, buy this. You might have to know a little bit about terminals though; you can actually play it without knowing it at all but it might give you a harder time, especially if you don't like to learn and read.[/i]

review_text_raw:
I think of Hacknet as a spiritual successor to Uplink, it has a good blend of fresh ideas and features borrowed from Uplink. When I compare the two, I view Hacknet as the more realistic game, whereas Uplink is more Hollywood styled. 

Hacknet features real Linux/UNIX commands, as well as real port numbers, Port 21 for FTP, Port 22 for SSH, 1433 for SQL etc. Now playing this won't teach you how to hack but it kind of gives you an idea of how it works, each system has a set number of ports that have to be open before you an crack it. Some of the later game systems have Proxy servers and Firewalls. Proxies can be overcome by opening a shell on 3-4 computers and telling them to spam it with junk traffic and data, meaning that it will allow unchecked traffic through, whereas Firewalls take a bit more time, you have to analyse it and doing so will reveal some characters, once you think you've got it you type SOLVE [FIREWALL SOLUTION] and it will check to see if it matches. 

Some tools can be run while a Proxy is up, but not while a Firewall is active and some can't be run with a Proxy active but they work while a Firewall is up. 
Each tool has it's own visual effect while it works and they're all beautifly done. My favorites being PortHack and SQL_Mem_Corrupt. 

The game is a bit more linear compared to Uplink, in Hacknet you're forced into the story as soon as the game begins, whereas with Uplink the story kicks in a couple of weeks into the game after some freelance work.

Hacknet has some intresting things to search for though, certain documents such as IRC logs are pretty funny. 

Overall though I'd say it's worth the buy, espiecally due to it getting a free multiplayer and some DLC content later in the year. And the soundtrack fits the game extremely well.

And for those who are intrested, the font used in the >HACKNET_ title can be found here: http://www.dafont.com/kremlin.font?text=HACKNET

review_text_raw:
Steam needs to update the rating system. This thumbs up/down is just too simplistic. While I do recommend the game for those who never played a hack "sim" before, I get the feeling that some people who are used to Uplink will be disappointed.

Uplink is the only game like this one I've played, and Hacknet is obviously inspired by it, so this is basically a comparison between the 2.

If you played Uplink this will be a walk in the park. Aside from visuals, there's nothing here that Uplink didn't do better back in 2001. With the excepton of a couple of moments, all missions are exactly the same all the way through, so it gets repetitive quite fast. 

There's no sense of danger or urgency Uplink gives you. Nobody will come after you, there's no police, companies you hack won't give a shit. Despite of what the game tells you right at the beggining, there's no need to cover your tracks. In Uplink, everytime you hack into a system it's a race against time. In Hacknet there's nothing like it. Once you block a trace you can spend as much time as you want in any system.

There's no rig upgrades, no rewards, nothing like it. You just complete the mission, get a "thank you" email and move on to the next.  

Both games have a story, but Uplink is more of a sandbox. After you get the hang of it you can do whatever you want and follow the story whenever you want. Hacknet, on the other hand, is pretty linear. That's a big dissapointment, specially after a great "wtf do I do now" moment right in the beggining. After that, you get the feeling you're never safe, but unfortunately nothing like that ever happens again. Storywise, Uplink is way more interesting, while Hacknet is cliche and way too simplistic.

That's the main problem with this game. It's way too easy. Uplink is infuriating unforgiven to the player. Once you start to mess with big companies, one small screw up means game over. Add that to the fact that the game is pretty much a roguelike, so it's not like you can go back to a previous save, you have to start all over again. In Hacknet, you don't need to worry about that. Like I said before, there's no need to clean after you. If you get caught, all you need to do is change your ip adress.

Anyway, if you never played a hacking "sim" before, this might be a good place to start. Like Uplink, It's really easy to get into, you don't need to now anything about code to play both games, and they give you a good sense of immersion.   

Hacknet has a good concept, but is way too simple for those looking for a challenge. I hope the "Labyrinths" expansion adds more substance to the game.

5/10

review_text_raw:
[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.

review_text_clean: [h1] Hacknet [/h1] [b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b] [h1] Run-through [/h1] Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web. With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines. [h1] Pros: [/h1] • Amazing story • Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up • Challenging and entertaining puzzles • The music feels always on point with the situation • Mod support • Tons of fun little Easter Eggs [h1] Cons: [/h1] • The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre • As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences [h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1] [u][b] General information [/b][/u] Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job. Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere. There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth. Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program. The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games. Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there. [u][b] Content [/b][/u] Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay. [h1] Technical Analysis [/h1] [u][b] Graphics [/b][/u] A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else. Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text. [u][b] Music [/b][/u] For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions. [u][b] HUD [/b][/u] The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable. To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other. [u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u] None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done. [h1] Wrapping up [/h1] Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for. review_text_raw:
First of all, I never played Uplink, so I can't compare this to that. What I did play was the HackRUN saga, so please pardon my comparison to a not very similar game. I also think it's funny that there are .dll and .exe file on what is (seemingly) a Linux system, but I can ignore that.

In a nutshell, Hacknet is a hacking sim game with a decent storyline. That is something I don't see often. HackRUN also has a storyline, but it's pretty linear if you ask me. This game uses real UNIX commands. For those of you new to the coding world (I guess?), it won't be hard to pick up; the tutorial does a good job of introducing the commands, and the 'help' menu will always be there to help you. For those of you who are familiar with the UNIX command prompt, you will be pleasantly surprised. The animations you get when hacking is pretty cool too. The best part of this games\ is that there are some systems that will start tracing you once you start your hacks. You have 100 seconds to do whatever you need to do and GTFO the system, or else (I don't actually know what happens because I have never failed doing so). You can, disconnect midway to cut the trace short and come back in the system again to do your stuff (again) at a later time, but hey, where's the fun in that? Along the way of making yourself a name in the hacking world (in the game), you will encounter files that are seemingly unimportant (like IRC log files, random text files, etc.). You are half right, [b]most[/b] of these files are unimportant. They may contain jokes and the stupidity of internet friends chatting together; but the rest may contain passwords that will make your life much easier when attempting to access some systems or useful information on your target's location.

There are decent puzzles in this game that happens in a specific scenario, but the contracts you get are pretty repetitive: [spoiler]probe the system, bypass proxy/firewall if those are there, open some ports, hack in, do your stuff, clear logs, get out[/spoiler]. New commands are introduced every now and then, but those have instructions along with them, so it's pretty easy to do whatever you need to do after. Basically, it's not very challenging (unless the devs add a "No x-server" mode to force you to use the command prompt throughout the game, that would be really fun, devs pls read). The last thing that this game lacks is the ability to adjust the SFX volume. Me clicking things actually shocks me sometimes because trust me, the SFXs are loud.

In conclusion, Hacknet is a good hacking sim with a decent storyline and a bit of realism. Would I recommend? Yes. Would I play again? Yes.

If you reach this point, thank you for raking your time to read the massive wall of text that my review is (lol).

review_text_raw:
A very introspective look at UNIX commands and the general actions of hacking - which is basically accurate, but taking out the time required to accomplish these things (for example, you can solve port protocols within a few seconds, but IRL this might take hours).

Basically, if you want the "reality" where you are the hacker in one of these movies (you're not playing the hacker, but ARE the hacker), then this is pretty spot-on. It just removes most of the tedium of the acitivites. This is not to say that the game isn't repetitive; it is, and remains true to its roots as a simulator. By nature, most simulators run off of repetitive actions which require muscle memory and timing in order to complete.

In actual fact, this is more of a puzzle-solving game. However, combined with some funny easter eggs (IRC chats can get hilarious) and honest-to-god methodology on the principles of hacking, this actually becomes enjoyable unless you just want to shoot things in the face (in which case, this is NOT the game for you).

Anyone who wants to work in software QA should be able to play this game comfortably, figure out most of the puzzles, and genuinely enjoy the experience. If you can't, don't take QA as a career. Because this in almost any form is what you do - all day, every day. I know this from 14 years of experience at that job in everything from game development to SAS or security software.

There are a few points I wish there were more of, or more developed. As game, it's pretty linear. There are nice little things like finding additional information on a server which gives you another terminal to hack, or a phone to break into, but these are too few and far between. It could be far more sandboxy if there were a freeform mode for points, which had sets of systems and connected devices which would allow you to randonly investigate things you found on another system. In this, you'd need a points system or something to gain (money, cred, whatever) - which would be a welcome addition to the game. I think another fun mode would be to actually use the system specs for the computer it was running on for memory, etc. as well as randonly generating in-game groups to become involved with, do missions for (from forums, etc.)

I recommend this game, just due to the simulation nature being captured very well. That being said, this game won't be for everyone. Much of the game is tedium and random investigation - which is exactly what hacking is about. One of the best missions which represents this is the "Project Junebug" mission. You're basically let loose to figure out how to accomlish the task, you have a lot of reading to do to catch up on how to accomplish it, and there isn't any handholding. YOU have to do the tasks, to the best of your understanding, and figure out indeed, what those tasks are, and it involves multiple servers, and different methods of having the same outcome.

review_text_raw:
This was incredibly thrilling to play. The push for speed challenged your ability to retain information in a short period of time, and it was an incredible experience. It's not real coding, like others have mentioned, so you're not going to learn anything. You essentially learn how to use prebuilt tools in a command prompt and how to communicate with a computer. But it works like a virtual machine with its own language and a fake operating system. (And I think that's really cool). It's also pretty cool that you can see your actual computer's command prompt when you minimize the game, essentially seeing how this virtual machine is talking to your computer.

However, there are gripes.

The ability to lock yourself out of beating the game without knowing it is really easy. You have to be VERY mindful of your actions. Deleting the wrong thing can trap you and force you to start a new game entirely.  

There are also some bugs, mostly involving how the quest system operates. That can also get stuck, especially if you already have a grasp of what you need to do, you can outrun your quest and cause it to lock up. Pace yourself.

Lastly, having content that is procedurally generated is awesome, but I felt like the game struggled between being "open world" and linear. If you want a game where you can investigate to find the story, open world is a wonderful option, but a linear story is great too if you're immersive enough.

Overall, if you want an experience that's an "idea" of hacking, you should definitely try this game.

If the developers make another game like this, I'd be interested in playing that one too. Maybe a sequel? I love the concept, but I'd really hope for a more open world experience.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is an excellent hacking simulator. Its user interface is very convincing and sleek, and there is just enough recognizable computer-jargon to make it somewhat realistic without making it boring or too dense to understand. Using the command terminal is way faster (and way cooler) then just using the GUI and makes you feel like you're the real deal.

Downsides to the game are the occasional spelling mistakes and the lack of explanation at some points in the game. My biggest issue with the game, however, is the complete linearity of the game. It never feels like you're interacting with a bigger world around you, just a pre-determined set of servers you have to hack, which is a shame. If it could be expanded somewhat to include a more dynamic 'internet' for you to explore, and more leeway in how to approach missions, this would've been the new standard in hacking sims. As is, it's a great game, but Uplink still holds the title.

review_text_raw:
[h1][b]IF YOU LIKE THE IDEA OF A GAME FOCUSING ENTIRELY ON A TERMINAL/COMMAND-LINE AND SOME EASY TO MODERATELY DIFFICULT PUZZLES THROWN IN, YOU MAY LIKE THIS GAME.[/b][/h1]
As someone who has a bit of experience with the UNIX terminal and commands, this game had my absolute full attention and felt familiar to me. [b]I've just recently bought this game (yesterday, at the time of writing) and I was absolutely HOOKED and couldn't get away from it. Hacknet is absolutely my style of game! (right now, I've just beaten the base game and will go through the DLC content shortly. but I may fiddle around with the Extensions)[/b]

[h1][b]TARGET[/b][/h1]
Obviously, this game isn't for everyone. A terminal-based game can seem intimidating or uninteresting to someone who has no experience with it before (and even if you do, a terminal-based game may not be that interesting). If the screenshots and description provided by the game do not capture your attention, it's probably not the game for you. But if your curiosity is piqued, it may be a great experience for you.

[h1][b]PUZZLE ELEMENTS AND TUTORIALS[/b][/h1]
Hacknet introduces itself quite well to the uninformed, and doesn't hand-hold. It throws you straight in after a short tutorial on using the terminal and interface, therefore encouraging experimentation with what you have available. By not holding the player's hand, succeeding in the puzzles without any additional help besides what the game provides will give you a sense of accomplishment. However, that can turn some people off, and if it does, it may not be for you.

It is possible to get stuck in several points in the game, but no solution is too far out there and is solvable without a walkthrough. (and I admit, I have, and have consulted a walkthrough but I was extra careful not to look any further ahead than the current task at hand, most of the time I had just forgotten something simple and was able to get back on track quickly).

The puzzles start off pretty easy, leading you on and increasing the difficulty as it goes, pretty much gently guiding you on how to work with the game's unique nature.

At certain times, the tasks can seem repetitive, and to be fair, it is. You are constantly trying to break into a lot of different computers, servers, devices, etc. but that's what it is. It is an accurate representation instead of the flashy Hollywood style hacking seen on film (but it certainly can be flashy when it wants to be and is for certain parts).

[h1][b]STORY[/b][/h1]
The story itself is nothing outstanding, but it certainly fits the theme and style of the game. It's perfect for the game. The story is there for the beginning and the end of your gameplay, giving you purpose to start and an objective to reach near the end. In the middle of the game, you are given freedom to do what you wish. Or PointClicker, if that's your thing (I won't judge!).

[h1][b]MUSIC[/b][/h1]
The music is an absolute fit for Hacknet and I often found myself focusing on the killer beats rather than what's at hand. It also made me quite shaky during the parts that are time-based.

[h1][b]OVERALL[/b][/h1]
Overall, Hacknet is extremely accurate compared to other things that have tried to display this kind of topic before. The elements work wonderfully and the balance between gameplay and the real elements is on point (all the commands given are used at one point or another and no unnecessary garbage is there). To the average person who may not know anything about the terminal, it can be exciting to get into it for the first time not knowing anything and eventually learn (there may be a little higher risk of getting stuck at a point, but that's okay!). To those who are a little familiar with the terminal and commands, you'll feel right at home and understand the game quickly and have a great time with it!

[h1][b]SHOULD YOU GET IT?[/b][/h1]
If this game looks interesting, [b]IT WILL BE FOR YOU.[/b] The terminal looks intimidating from the start, and if that doesn't deter you and the description of the game brings you in further, you [b]WILL[/b] enjoy it!

review_text_raw:
I normally don't like puzzle games, because eventually a puzzle loses me once and then I never get back into the groove. Hacknet is possibly the first puzzle game that I have enjoyed since the days of Popcap. It helps that it is usually very easy, as long as you have experience with computers, and gives you specific instructions as to how to beat the levels beyond "hack everything you can". 
I have only two gripes. First is that the RAM management aspect (you only have a limited amount of ram, so you have to figure out the best parallel computing strategies when you're under a time limit) also cuts into your note-taking extensively. A single paragraph of notes takes up so much RAM that you can only use the smaller programs until you get it out of your face. The boss level fell flat as a pancake after I lost because I couldn't remember the name of a program that I needed and the list I had written for just such an occasion was deleted for taking up too much RAM. Why even have notes make such an impact on RAM economy if the player can just open up the notepad on his real desktop and use that?
Besides that bizarre choice, the network UI is appaling. In the screenshots, all those dots in the bottom of the screen are computers, there is no way to see what they are without mousing over them, you can't move them around, and they frequently overlap each other. That's another way the boss level fell flat: I just quit midway through because I had accidentally spent half the timer hacking the server that it had been placed on top of. You are just expected to remember where everything is, which wasn't easy when I had another game session the very next day, so I bet it's hellish if you have to wait a week to get back into it.
As for the good parts, it is very cool that you can play the entire game through console if you want to. Of particular note are the commands to open and close the CD tray. Apparently they actually work, even in multiplayer. There's even a branching storyline, as well as a substantial library of mods which are still being added to to this day. If you like the gameplay, then you can keep going until you don't anymore without having to retread the same ground more than a few times.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a rare gem in the indie scene—a game that doesn't just simulate hacking, but immerses you in it with a level of authenticity and atmosphere that most genre attempts barely graze. Designed by Team Fractal Alligator, it's a terminal-based hacking simulator where you dive deep into a rabbit hole of digital espionage, underground networks, and cryptic puzzles, all communicated through a command-line interface. On paper, that may sound dry. In execution, it’s anything but.

What makes Hacknet such a standout experience, is its faithfulness to real-world logic without alienating player unfamiliar with coding. It teaches by doing, never hand-holding but never abandoning you either. You’ll boot systems, probe for vulnerabilities, crack passwords, and manipulate files—all with just a blinking cursor and your wits. There’s a certain thrill in executing a flawless sequence of commands under pressure, like defusing a bomb with only seconds to spare.

The most positive  consistently praise its atmosphere. The soundtrack—moody and immersive—drenches every hack in tension and mystery. The narrative, while not overly complex, feeds a constant sense of curiosity. You're not just following orders; you're unraveling a digital conspiracy. Describe the experience as “empowering,” especially for those who’ve never touched a line of code before. There’s a genuine sense of growth as you become more fluent in your digital arsenal.

That said, even the best-crafted code has bugs. Point out a few frustrating limitations. First, while the UI is stylistically perfect for the theme, it can become visually fatiguing over long sessions, especially when you're staring at lines of text with minimal interface variety. Second, once you grasp the core mechanics, the challenge can taper off. Some missions fall into predictable patterns, and may find the mid-to-late game lacking in complexity.

Additionally, the lack of real choice in how you approach objectives can feel constricting. While it feels like a sandbox at first glance, the game often funnels you into single-solution puzzles. Wishing for more freedom to experiment or “break the system” in creative ways.

Hacknet is a brilliant idea executed with style, but not without cracks in its shell. The story is intriguing, yet occasionally shallow; the pacing tight, though at times undermined by repetitiveness. Still, it’s universally acknowledged as an educational and atmospheric triumph, especially for those willing to sink into its digital depths.

Final Verdict:
Hacknet is a thinking person’s game—a methodical, immersive dive into the world of virtual infiltration. It empowers through minimalism, teaches through tension, and wraps it all in a darkly ambient package. Despite a few structural shortcomings, it stands tall as a uniquely engrossing experience.

Rating: 8.5/10
A captivating digital puzzle-box, slightly constrained by its own structure, but well worth unlocking.

Amazing game. Definitely feels like a long-due spiritual successor to Uplink. Improves on it in a lot of ways, too; for example, by requiring the player to use a command-line interface rather than just clicking and dragging widgets around. It's also really fun and the soundtrack is pretty bitchin'.

Okay, now for the criticisms.

First, the game is way too easy and straightforward. Hacking every system can essentially be boiled down into three steps: take down firewall/proxy, open ports, run magical hacking tool. Missions are similarly straightforward: once you Hack into the Mainframe™ you dig around for clues, and if that fails, use your magical scan tool. Sometimes you're on a timer. And so on.

Second, missions are way too linear and the progression is kinda bugged. You are automatically assigned one mission at any given moment, and canceling it breaks the game by preventing you from proceeding to the next story-important mission. Some missions, e.g. the /el sidequest line, don't even trigger unless you meet some very specific criteria, and you can't backtrack to it later on. And even on the final set of missions, you can't even complete it unless you track down one very specific piece of software from a specific quest line which may or may not be available to you before the story-critical mission is forced upon you.

Third, a lot of hacking is just waiting for your damn magical programs to crack open ports and passwords for you after typing stuff into the command line. Which is boring, especially considering there usually isn't much of a challenge to begin with.

Anyway it's still a good game and I have zero regrets about throwing money at it.

review_text_raw:
Ever watched a hacking sequence in a movie and thought it looked equal parts ridiculous and cool? Hacknet leans into that fantasy while bringing the learning curve down to something genuinely manageable. Even a passing familiarity with command line will make this click, and if you have none at all, the in-game guidance and Steam's community resources fill in the gaps. Don't let the aesthetic intimidate you — it's far more approachable than it looks, and more fun and challenging than I expected.

I originally attempted this back in 2019 and bounced off it. Coming back now and having forgotten nearly everything I knew turned out to be a blessing. This was my first real dive into a command-line driven game, and while there is a GUI available for when you blank on specific commands or syntax, you'll spend most of your time in the terminal. The game gives you everything you need — but only if you actually read and retain the instructions when they appear. I found myself referencing help commands repeatedly and still making mistakes, which is entirely on me rather than the game. It's patient with you, as long as you're patient with it.

Progress doesn't always feel linear, which threw me at first, but it's part of the appeal. Every device you breach opens up a small world of its own — old chat rooms, private email exchanges between people living secret lives, someone just trying to organize a D&D session. The incidental storytelling is often genuinely funny, and the referenced media scattered throughout is a welcome discovery. The broader narrative — working your way up through hacker organizations, breaching servers to obtain, remove, or alter data — takes roughly three quarters of the runtime to fully reveal itself, but what surrounds it keeps things moving.

The soundtrack deserves particular attention. Sourced through Boss Battle Records across a range of artists — Carpenter Brut being the most familiar name — it's superb from start to finish. What makes it exceptional for a 2015 release is how dynamically it shifts and adapts based on what's happening in-game. I've already added it to regular rotation well after finishing.

At $10 full price and as low as $1.50 on sale, there's genuinely nothing to debate. Bundle it if you can, buy it regardless if you can't. Don't let the look of it put you off. 88/100

The incidental storytelling is often genuinely funny, and the referenced media scattered throughout is a welcome discovery. The broader narrative — working your way up through hacker organizations, breaching servers to obtain, remove, or alter data — takes roughly three quarters of the runtime to fully reveal itself, but what surrounds it keeps things moving. The soundtrack deserves particular attention. Sourced through Boss Battle Records across a range of artists — Carpenter Brut being the most familiar name — it's superb from start to finish. What makes it exceptional for a 2015 release is how dynamically it shifts and adapts based on what's happening in-game. I've already added it to regular rotation well after finishing. At $10 full price and as low as $1.50 on sale, there's genuinely nothing to debate. Bundle it if you can, buy it regardless if you can't. Don't let the look of it put you off. 88/100

I'll admit, I was not expecting much from a free humble game, especially one developed by a single person. Yet, I am plesantly suprised by the gameplay overall. This game is a hacking-puzzle game with a story essentially. 

When it comes to the hacking part, the mechanics feel cool to use and at times when hacking servers it can get intense and the learning curve as a result is well made. 

The puzzle part is also great, the game will tell you what you need to initally do in a mission and what the end goal is, but it heavily relies on your past experience with game mechanics and a bit of snooping on files to navigate through a misson.

The story itself is a 7.5 out of 10 but the story telling is 9 out of 10. To get the story in this game, you'll have to snoop on files like you would do in regular missons, with some files pointing in other directions for more bits of the story and since you are already conditioned to snoop around, the way the story is told fits the context well.

Replayability is quite good, passwords, usernames (non generic ones) and a bunch of information in missions is randomly generated which can be refreshing, but also the game has multiple paths with an obvious linear path and a secretive path which means you'll be going back to the game to find its secrets. 

It also has some humorous parts of the game which did may be giggle a bit.

I only have a couple issues:

- The saving system is a one slot system, so when I was at the point in the story where the secret path can be taken I couldn't make two game saves, and for the sake of the story line I went with the normal path on my first go.
- On some themes (the way the UI is arranged) tags on the map appear to be unreadable due to the names being cut off
- Achievement recognition is buggy, if you are a completionist, better prepare to pull your hair out

Got this game because it was on sale and I was interested in it being a hacking game. I was not disappointed and would pay full price for it hands down. By no means is this game super realistic, but it is definitely intriguing and fun. It uses some real Unix commands, and has a little sense of how hacking works in the real world, however it is still a game... but it felt like so much more than that. No prior hacking/computer science experience or knowledge is needed. The game teaches you from the get go with a tutorial on the basics of how to hack nodes in the game and a few of the commands you can use. All you have to do is type "help" if you forget a command. Also you can autofill commands with the tab key which really saves you some time.

The story is very captivating. There's quite a bit of plot to uncover all while you're exploring the network of loads of IPs. It's not exactly a sandbox but you do have a bit of freedom when it comes to certain missions or hacking methods. Every step of the way this game keeps you sucked in until you finally uncover every hole you can find. Once I got to the end, my mind was blown.

I currently have 16 hours in this game. I just started the Labyrinths DLC which is already proving to be worth the buy as well. You get different background music, more GUI themes, and brand new story and collection of nodes to explore. Once I finish the DLC I am definitely going back in for another playthrough. 

Overall I would give this game a 9/10. Some parts may seem a tad bit repetitive. But the game definitely makes up for it with a great dense story, killer music, and the awesome feeling of being immersed into a world where you can become an expert hacker

Awesome fun, highly recommend if you enjoyed Uplink or are looking for a "cinematic hacking game". You primarily interact with the game through a command-line interface, so I hope you're comfortable typing quickly and accurately under stress. There is an autofill that helps negate this somewhat, but it only does some of the work for you.

The game is pretty straightforward with a few standout moments where it really opens up and shows its potential. For example, in an early-game mission, you get hacked and you can either choose to steal what you need back and leave it at that or you can hunt them down and punish them for what they did to you. There is another, later mission where you're basically given free reign in to solve a more complex problem (there's only one real solution, but there are a lot of ways of getting to it). If there were more missions like that, or it were a bit more open-ended, I'd easily call the game a 10/10. As it is, it's a bit linear, with potential for only 2 playthroughs (depending on how you handle the hack from the beginning).

I have yet to get the Labyrinths DLC, but I intend to buy it as soon as I can, as I feel it will help cut down on the sameness the gameplay gets.

After playing Uplink back in the day in college, I never really found another hacking simulator that I enjoyed....until Hacknet.  This game is, while it has faults, is definitely now a classic.  

Primarily, the game is a puzzle game that adds interactive fiction, role-playing, non-linear sandbox design, minimal technical skills, and heavy analytical skills (largely needed for the non-linear approaches).  For those that are technical, there may much more linearity but there is still enough guesswork for good exploration.  Ultimately, the game does an excellent job at putting you in the roll of a hacker and while there may be similar commands, the technical pieces are really dumbed down and do get repetitive (a real script kiddie would you know....write scripts).  It is this roleplay that I think the game excels.  I don't want to say too much because that would be spoilerly.

Definitely going to be buying Labryinths.

P.S. Pro-tip: look up how to hack your seetings to use a Grid for your nmap...I learned the trick way too late. :)

despite my playtime as of the review, ive enjoyed the game. its great! in my opinion, worth the price. sure, it has its vices, what game doesnt? the game isnt realistic to real life hacking, but i think its hard to make a game thats realistic and fun when it comes to hacking and/or programming games as it will be only for a specific audience which reduces who would play and enjoy the game by alot. its a bit repetitive with how hacking to most systems is the same, but i enjoyed many puzzles that this game provided, especially in the labyrinth DLC. this game isnt perfect, no game is but id say its honestly the closest of any games of this genre that i played. the music is one of the few game soundtracks that i actually liked and would listen to in my spare time. the multiple times that arent just port openers are fun and useful!... well most of them (looking at you, Clock.exe). but id say that some are underused, like the log creator and opener, theyre required to be used i think 2-3 times, but the gap between their uses is too big which makes those tools easily forgettable and can make some puzzles hard to impossible without googling how to solve them. id also say that the map can sometimes be hard to use with time, as if youre looking for a specific server, its hard to find it due to there being so many, even with the map organiser tool provided in the labyrinth DLC. i also love how the trace mechanic isnt an immediate game over like in other hacking games where there are also traces, instead you get a saving grace thats (in my opinion) too easy to complete once youve done it once as the process doesnt change if you need to do it many times. i also love how you can use either the GUI or visual part to play the game or the terminal, you are rarely forced to use either. the many customisation options are very fun and well made, they give you a fresh look at your game, either just changing how it looks to where some things are placed. and then theres the story, now im not an emotional personal and ill admit, i havent cried at the ending but i loved it and felt sorry for our favorite guy, especially after the ending cutscene. i had to replay the game to realise that what he meant is that the remaining copy is ours, the actual game. the labyrinth dlc also messes with the games directory, i would have loved to see more of this mechanic but i more than understand why it isnt used as it would likely get annoying. i also really like how there are what i presume are steam keys, i doubt there are any unredeemed keys after 8 years so i dont know what the keys are for, but its a nice gesture. the dev speaking to us after completing the game and letting us know the ips for some fun servers like "cheaters stash" basically letting us get most binary files (port openers and trace stopper) and others. the labyrinths ending is definitely an unexpected twist and while the choice doesnt matter its still nice to have one. i also immensely enjoyed the labyrinth DLC (if you havent noticed already), i enjoyed how the mission and hub actually looked like and the addition of letting us communicate with the others despite our inability to speak. it could also potentially be used if there was a multiplayer, like a race or trying to speedrun many preset missions, either trying to help or stall your friends and you could communicate as a nice feature, maybe making info on server1 vital to help solve a puzzle on server2 or something like that. also the amount of secrets or easter eggs there are is a very nice and fun addition. the shells are imo underused and their trap is rarely used, i think i used it like once or twice on my second playthrough and it actually did something. and there are the fan made DLCs which is great, you can still play even after you complete the actual game.

In short: i enjoyed the game very much, the characters (which are unfortunately few) are lovable. the game has its vices but those are few and often just mild annoyances. ill definitely be replaying the game and its DLC aswell as the fan made ones. its worth its price, but if you think its not for you, you can wait for a discount.

[b][h1]I almost wanted to write this as a negative review.[/h1][/b]
However, on balance, I switched the direction of that thumb.

Full disclosure: I am a professional sysadmin, and I Tux and I are old buddies. He didn't like me at first, but I pulled his source and patched it, and now he [b]loves[/b] me. 

[h1] First the things that drove me up the wall...[/h1]

Mostly, it was the [b]almost[/b] unix commands, like 'RM *' instead of 'rm -r -f' and things like supporting tab completion and wildcards but [i]not[/i] partial names [i]with[/i] wildcards. I can't tell you how many times muscle memory had me type 'RM @32[Tab]*' to delete all logs that began with @3213 - but this does [i]not[/i] work in-game. You either delete everything, or have to type in each file one at a time. Fortunately, this ultimately proved irrelevant after I later discovered all other in-game admins use their keyboards only as a protective drool mat for their desks (more on that below.)

Also, the fact that you could just RM * and expect that the sysadmin on the system wouldnot find it suspicious at all that the system lacks logs of any kind for a whole time perod, and the last log is a x.x.x.x disconnected with no matching 'connected' message. Nope. Nothing suspicious there.

Almost makes me ashamed of wearing a white hat in real life. 

[h1]Kudos to the devs to for trying to acquaint us with RFC1700, but...[/h1]

What I found silly and pointless was to use real port numbers that you'd exepct to see in real life servers (22 for ssh, etc) but making you type in the port numbers for your magic 'sploit to work against (where there is never any deviation [i][b]ever[/b][/i] from the standard) is just silly as well.

[i]Note: I guess the IANA in-game must have been OK with that company creating the protocol that uses port 104, as that is in the range of ports they control assignments for... Just sayin' [/i]

I would assume a hacker as talented as 'bit' that could write a magic rootkit could figure out that if I didn't provide a port number for an SSH exploit, that it should just assume something as reasonable as, oh... assuming that the ssh daemon is running on port 22 like every. single. system. in the game's universe.

[h1]Word to the devs: It's either 'magic' hacking, or it's realistic. Pick your direction and don't try to do both at once.[/h1]

I guess my complaints kind of revolved around the fence sitting. Why go to all that trouble to get many technical details right, but still use hacking tools that so advanced as to appear 'magic' but at the same time retarded in so many easily fixed ways.

They even showed enough 'nix savvy to use tools like ps and kill mostly accurately and to cleverly make 'nmap' the command to trigger a scan for listening ports.

[b]Ironically, I guess that proves Bit's programming skills are a bit hit or miss (pun intended.)[/b] He did make nmap not require all its real-life complicated arguments and just assume you were doing an active port scan against the host you were connected to.

Those kind of professional pedantic nitpicks are why I wanted so badly to make this a negative review.

But not everyone is a professional sysadmin, and probably wouldn't have known or cared because they don't know better.

[h1]I am forced to admit, though...[/h1]
It's actually a very fun game. I applaud them for trying so hard to simulate the use of the command line where real sysadmins work. I also applaud them for at least trying to make people aware of the principles of security (or insecurity, as it were.)

I think it was worth the money. Nobody that doesn't live in my professional circles would be bothered by things like not being able to cd from one subdirectory directly to another because the GUI is so much easier and more convenient for this anyway.

If they would just have fixed the parser to accept partial wildcards and made the opposing sysadmins not complete clowns, I would have enjoyed it more.

On balance: 8/10 would be frustrated by the lack of being able to chain 'CD /logs && RM * && dc'  all over again.

Full disclosure: I am a giant nerd. Grew up more on computers (and dogs!) than, like, ya know.... PEOPLE... The point is, if you put a terminal or a shell in front of me I get super excited and it's instantly, like, +5,000 to appreciation for thing.

ANYWAY.

This game is sublime. I think, oftentimes, if you look up hacking sims, you get to get stuff like Uplink, which is very good, certainly, and I DO recommend it, but Hacknet was made as a spiritual successor to it (by the dev's own confirmation), and I consider it better in every way. Uplink is a little more sandbox-y (think, like, a game that is entirely a radiant quest from Skyrim. Except, like... good. And dynamic); Hacknet actually has a story. There are a number of missions to do, and it's not linear in the sense that you have to do everything in order, but there are a couple factions you can go with and you'll get different tasks from them. It all culminates in the same storyline at the end, but I don't mean that as a negative. The writing is really good, the gameplay is engaging, and there are tons of little incidentals you can find for worldbuilding and extraneous fun (IRC logs are a really good example of this, and many of those are extremely well-observed; tech-heads, I can guarantee, will find some gems in there).

Essentially, you encounter external systems and learn to crack them. For various reasons. Everything from "delete this sensitive file" to "modify a file's contents" to "find out where this signal came from" to "cripple this server" and others. And that's just for starters. Eventually you start dealing with conspiracies, and your missions get really involved, having to crack multiple terminals, finding links between them, worming your way into other systems, finding user credentials, reading e-mails, finding synched external devices, etc, etc. You have to break through security before you can CRACK the system, naturally, and different systems have different layers requiring different programs to surpass. It's almost entirely SKiddying, for those of you who are also dorks like myself, but it's very entertainingly-done and the graphics built to illustrate Computer Happenings (R)(C) are really rad. I wouldn't be surprised if you needed a guide at some point, your first time through, but, well, put it this way: collaboration between agents is pretty common, so don't feel bad.

The interface is really cool, you CAN do just about everything with the mouse, if you're wired that way, but you can also use the console, which is my preferred way of doing things. There are multiple .sys overlays you can enable, as well, to change your GUI and layout, which adds a little customization (some of them done by commissioned artist). The expansion that's since come out is a lot of fun, and adds probably another four to six hours to a game that I'd say is around ten hours your first time through, if you know what you're doing. Decently replayable, too.

Finally, I will say that this is one of my favorite soundtracks I've ever heard. I've never seen a game before this that uses Vaporwave as its backing, but it makes a lot of sense; that's a really good genre for focus-demanding work, like this game presents. Also, they used HOME on the soundtrack, and they are one of my absolute favorites (shill, shill). I will also say, while the OST is extremely chill, they DO use one of the higher-octane tracks from Hotline Miami 2, and I daresay it fits even better here.

All in all, you can get the game, its expansion, and both OSTs for twenty bucks, when it ISN'T on sale, and I find that to be a friggin' steal. On a closing note, there's no other game that will actually get your adrenaline pumping entering text commands at a shell. I defy anyone who says they can do the endgame of the original or Labyrinths without a significant spike in vitals.

UPDATE - A couple of days after I post this review, the developer announces that he patched the bug that made the game impossible to complete. While another bug does exist at present (where if you do not accept the Junebug mission in time, you lose the opportunity to continue with the main story), it is possible to work around this by reloading an old save.

Upon reaching the end of the game, I am absolutely convinced that this game is one of (if not) the best hacking simulators on the market. The final mission in the game is so intense. I had to do it in several parts and my heart was racing each time I started it. There was nothing I could suggest to make the gameplay itself any better. Maybe adding in more missions to give it some replayability and a bit more freedom to go off and hack to your hearts content for good or for evil. However, that could be a DLC pack and can easily be added in. As the game stands, it deserves an 8/10, purely because it's still not perfect in terms of the bugs. However, they should be fixed soon given the dedication the dev has with this game.

- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

Let me be perfectly clear with this before you read any further. I LOVE Hacknet. It's a fantastic game and is definitely better than Uplink by a mile. The use of real computer commands makes it feel much more realistic and the storyline is pretty awesome to boot. Plus, the time limit you have when a trace counter starts rapidly going down and you're waiting for the password crack to finish so you can intercept the trace creates one heck of an adrenaline rush.

However I cannot recommend it as it is now. There is a single bug I have encountered that makes the game impossible to complete. I will try to avoid giving away any spoilers, so this will be a bit vague. Later in game you are required to take on a mission that is part of the main storyline. However, you do not choose when this mission comes to you. It is automatically sent to you in an email and I'm not 100% sure what the criteria is for it appearing. To complete it, you need an .exe file used to crack a specific port which is only available by taking on a side mission. However, this mission is locked and once again, I do not know what the criteria is to unlock it. So I tried to take on the other available missions in an attempt to unlock the one I needed. In order to do this, you must abort the main storyline mission. Aborting a mission means you can NEVER attempt it again, making it impossible to continue with the main storyline. While I discovered it is possible to obtain the .exe without the mission, following an online walkthrough to obtain the information needed to get it instead of getting it in game feels wrong on so many levels, especially since it's deeply hidden within this seemingly permanently locked mission.

So at this time, I can't recommend it. The game is good, but I haven't been able to finish it because of this bug. The developer seems to be quite willing to take feedback and work on it so if you're reading this, I eagerly await a patch for this game. I can't wait to finish it.
